title: What if Transferable Skills Don't Exist?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou revisits what she calls the most durable and consequential of the 'seven myths about education' from her 2013 book: the belief that skills like creativity, communication, problem-solving, and critical thinking exist as generic, transferable capacities rather than being tightly bound to specific domain knowledge. Her recurring rebuttal to the common career-switcher counterexample is to ask what the two industries actually were: someone moving fluidly from financial journalism to bank corporate communications succeeded because the domain knowledge overlaps, not because they possess portable 'communication skills,' whereas the same journalist attempting to become an oncologist would find those supposedly transferable skills useless. The piece's most striking contribution is tracing the myth's 19th-century roots in 'formal discipline' theory -- the belief, once applied to the study of ancient Greek, that mastering one sufficiently difficult subject sharpens the mind into a general-purpose tool -- and showing that this discredited theory directly shaped the 1854 Northcote-Trevelyan Report, the founding document of the British civil service, which recommended recruiting classics graduates and then rotating them frequently between departments on the assumption their sharpened generalist minds would transfer seamlessly. Christodoulou argues the myth's damage now extends well beyond classrooms into universities (which market degrees on 'transferable skills' she believes mostly function as pure signaling) and into a civil service still structurally organized, over 170 years later, around a psychological theory that has been debunked.
points: The recurring rebuttal to the career-switcher counterexample -- 'what were the two industries?' -- exposes that apparent skill transfer (financial journalist to bank communications) tracks domain-knowledge overlap, not generic ability, since the same person moving to oncology would find no such transfer at all.

The historical discovery that Britain's civil service was explicitly founded on now-debunked 'formal discipline' theory (the 1854 Northcote-Trevelyan Report's recommendation to recruit classics graduates and rotate them between departments) shows the transferable-skills myth isn't merely an education-sector error but a structural assumption baked into a national institution for over 170 years.

Christodoulou's claim that university degrees mostly function as a 'signal' rather than a transferable-skills-delivery mechanism directly challenges how higher education is marketed to prospective students and employers.

The essay's closing observation -- that 19th-century thinkers could 'airily assert something that made very little sense' and still be hailed as heroic intellects -- cautions against assuming past authorities were more rigorous simply because their ideas proved durable, since durability and correctness are shown here to be entirely separate properties.
quotes: I don't think transferable skills exist. I think skills like creativity, problem-solving, communication and critical thinking are tied to domain knowledge. This means it is possible to be a brilliant creative thinker in one specific domain, and a terribly uncreative thinker in another domain.

Let's say instead that you spent twenty years working for a newspaper as a financial journalist, and then you wanted to switch careers to work as an oncologist. Financial journalists and oncologists both need to communicate, solve problems and think creatively. So can the financial journalist switch easily? No, of course not.

In the 19th century, a lot of prominent thinkers supported the idea of "formal discipline" -- which was that by studying something really hard, you would train up your brain to be a razor-sharp tool capable of solving any problem. The preferred "really hard thing" back then was ancient Greek. But whilst Greek has gone out of fashion, the basic idea of studying one thing that can make you good at everything remains.

It recommended that the civil service recruit officials who had studied subjects like Greek and Latin at university, on the grounds that they would have razor-sharp minds that could be turned to any problem.

Universities sell their degree courses with the idea of transferable skills. I don't buy this: I think the value of a degree is mostly in the signal, not in either the specific content or the alleged "transferable skills".
Some of these ideas have been remarkably durable, with the result that we have organised some important parts of the British state around a concept that doesn't exist.
